newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan spokesman apologises for sex slave remarks.
newsitem.headline: Japan spokesman apologises for sex slave remarks.

text.p: Japan's government spokesman apologised on Monday for remarks that cast a shadow over the weekend summit between Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and South Korean President Kim Young-sam.
On Friday, Seiroku Kajiyama criticised a reference in Japanese junior high school textbooks to Asian women forced to provide sex for Japanese soldiers during World War Two.

Hashimoto had to start his talks with Kim by apologising for the remarks, in which Kajiyama had complained that textbooks were presenting the Japanese military's use of sex slaves, or "comfort women" in the Japanese euphemism, without providing the "social background".

"It is my fault and I apologise from the bottom of my heart that my remarks caused some unpleasant feeling at the Japan-South Korean summit and misunderstanding by the South Korean people," Kajiyama, the chief cabinet secretary, told a regular news conference.

He had told reporters during a briefing on the eve of the summit: "It is odd teaching (Japanese schoolchildren) about the comfort women issue without teaching the social background of the authorised prostitution system at that time."
About 200,000 captured "comfort women" from Korea, the Philippines, China, Indonesia and the Netherlands were forced into prostitution in one of World War Two's darker chapters.

Although Hashimoto apologised to Kim on Saturday, he appeared to roll back on Monday when referring to Kajiyama's remarks, telling reporters the spokesman had simply "explained the social background that in Japan in those days there was an authorised prostitution system".

Hashimoto is president of the ruling conservative Liberal Democratic Party, which contains a large nationalist faction which has fought to keep references to the sex slaves and other atrocities by the Japanese military out of school textbooks.
